DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash:
“Rash” is not a diagnosis — it is a starting point. The first question is never “what is it called?” but “is the patient sick, and are there red flags?” Fever with a non-blanching rash is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise → antibiotics now (see meningococcal disease, petechiae & purpura); a painful rash with mucosal erosions and blistering is Stevens-Johnson / toxic epidermal necrolysis — stop the drug (see dermatological emergencies); urticaria with airway or breathing compromise is anaphylaxis → IM adrenaline (see anaphylaxis); and >90% erythema is erythroderma (see erythroderma). Only once these are cleared do you describe the morphology (macular / papular, purpuric, vesicular / bullous, pustular, wheals, scaly plaques), the distribution and the time course, and route to the specific pattern — eczema, psoriasis, urticaria, a drug or viral exanthem (see eczema, psoriasis). SCAM: Site, Configuration, Arrangement, Morphology.
🚨Some rashes are emergencies. Look for the warning signs: a non-blanching purpuric rash with fever (meningococcal sepsis → benzylpenicillin now) (see meningococcal disease); skin pain / tenderness, mucosal involvement (mouth, eyes, genitals), blistering, skin detachment and a positive Nikolsky sign (SJS / TEN, or DRESS with fever, facial oedema and eosinophilia) — stop the culprit drug (see dermatological emergencies, blistering rash); urticaria with lip / tongue swelling, wheeze, stridor or hypotension (anaphylaxis) (see anaphylaxis); widespread erythema >90% with systemic upset (erythroderma); and rapidly spreading erythema with pain out of proportion (necrotising fasciitis) or monomorphic punched-out erosions on eczema (eczema herpeticum) (see skin infections).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Meningococcal sepsis
  • Fever + a non-blanching purpuric / petechial rash + systemically unwell
  • → immediate antibiotics (benzylpenicillin / ceftriaxone) + resuscitation, do not wait (see meningococcal disease, petechiae & purpura)
  • Glass (tumbler) test; may have meningism, shock
🚩SJS / TEN & drug emergencies
  • Painful rash + mucosal erosions (mouth, eyes, genitals) + blisters + skin detachment (Nikolsky+)
  • A drug trigger 1–3 weeks before — stop the culprit, dermatological emergency (see dermatological emergencies, blistering rash)
  • DRESS: fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia, organ involvement
🚩Anaphylaxis / angioedema
  • Urticaria + lip / tongue swelling, wheeze, stridor, hypotension
  • → IM adrenaline, ABC, remove trigger (see anaphylaxis, urticaria)
  • Rapid onset after food / drug / sting
🟠Erythroderma
  • >90% of the skin red and scaly + systemic upset
  • Fluid / heat / protein loss, high-output failure, sepsis risk (see erythroderma)
  • Causes: eczema, psoriasis, drugs, lymphoma (Sézary)
🟠Serious skin infection
  • Cellulitis (hot, spreading, tender erythema + fever) (see cellulitis)
  • Necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, crepitus, rapid) — surgical emergency
  • Eczema herpeticum (monomorphic punched-out erosions), staph scalded skin (see skin infections)
🩹Common inflammatory dermatoses
  • Eczema (itchy, flexural), psoriasis (scaly extensor plaques) (see eczema, psoriasis)
  • Urticaria (transient wheals), contact dermatitis (see contact dermatitis)
  • Viral exanthem, pityriasis rosea, lichen planus
Sick or not sick, first. Before naming a rash, screen for the emergencies: non-blanching + fever, mucosae + blisters + skin pain, urticaria + airway, >90% erythema. Everything else is described by morphology, distribution and time course.

3Assess & act
At the bedside — sick or not, blanching or not, the morphology and distribution
History & red flags
Onset and speed, fever / systemic upset, itch or pain; new drugs (1–3 weeks), infections, contacts, travel, atopy; mucosal, airway or joint symptoms; sun exposure; what makes it better / worse
Examine
Blanching? (glass test), morphology (macule / papule / vesicle / pustule / wheal / plaque / purpura), distribution & configuration; check mucosae, nails, scalp, palms / soles; Nikolsky sign; are they febrile / unwell, any airway compromise?
Investigate
Often clinical; for the unwell: FBC, CRP, U&E, LFTs, cultures / meningococcal PCR, eosinophils (DRESS); skin swab / viral PCR, skin biopsy for a blistering / uncertain rash, mast-cell tryptase after anaphylaxis, and targeted autoimmune / infection screens
Act
Treat the emergency first — antibiotics for meningococcal sepsis, IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis, stop the drug and refer SJS / TEN, supportive care for erythroderma; then treat the pattern — emollients / topical steroids for eczema, antihistamines for urticaria, antibiotics for cellulitis, and refer where the diagnosis is unclear

The rules that carry it: screen for the four emergencies (non-blanching + fever; mucosae + blisters; urticaria + airway; >90% erythema) before anything else. Then describe the rash — morphology, distribution, time course — and route to the pattern.

DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus:
Pruritus is the sensation that provokes scratching. The single most useful division is: is there a primary rash, or not? An itch with a rash is usually a skin disease — eczema, scabies, urticaria, lichen planus, dermatitis herpetiformis, bullous pemphigoid (see eczema, scabies, urticaria). An itch without a rash (skin normal apart from excoriations) points to a systemic cause: cholestasis (obstructive jaundice, primary biliary cholangitis) (see jaundice, primary biliary cholangitis), chronic kidney disease (uraemic) (see chronic kidney disease), iron deficiency and thyroid disease, haematological disease (polycythaemia — itch after a hot bath; Hodgkin lymphoma) (see polycythaemia, plethora, lymphoma), malignancy (paraneoplastic), drugs (opioids), HIV and pregnancy. Always look for the red-flag trio: lymphadenopathy, jaundice and weight loss.
🚨Persistent itch without a rash can be the first sign of serious disease. Think Hodgkin lymphoma (itch with night sweats, weight loss and rubbery lymphadenopathy) and other paraneoplastic itch (see lymphoma). Cholestatic itch with painless jaundice, pale stools and weight loss may be pancreatic or biliary cancer (see pancreatic cancer, jaundice). In pregnancy, itch of the palms and soles without a rash in the third trimester is intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy — a fetal risk needing bile acids and monitoring (see medical disorders in pregnancy). And aquagenic pruritus (itch after a warm bath) suggests polycythaemia vera (see polycythaemia).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Malignancy / lymphoma
  • Hodgkin lymphoma — itch + night sweats, weight loss, rubbery lymphadenopathy, alcohol-induced node pain
  • Paraneoplastic itch (also myeloproliferative, solid tumours) (see lymphoma)
  • Examine nodes, liver, spleen; FBC, LDH, imaging
🚩Cholestasis / biliary obstruction
  • Itch + jaundice, pale stools, dark urine, raised ALP / GGT (see jaundice)
  • Painless obstructive jaundice + weight loss = pancreatic / biliary cancer (see pancreatic cancer); PBC in a middle-aged woman (see primary biliary cholangitis)
  • Bile salts in the skin drive the itch
🚩Obstetric cholestasis
  • Pregnant, third trimester, itch of palms and soles — no rash
  • Raised bile acids / LFTs → fetal risk (stillbirth) — monitor + ursodeoxycholic acid (see medical disorders in pregnancy)
  • Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
🟠Systemic (renal / haem / endocrine)
  • Chronic kidney disease (uraemic itch) (see chronic kidney disease)
  • Polycythaemia vera (itch after a hot bath) (see polycythaemia, plethora); iron deficiency (see anaemia)
  • Thyroid disease (hyper / hypo) (see thyroid disease)
🩹Primary skin disease
  • Eczema (itchy, flexural), urticaria (wheals) (see eczema, urticaria)
  • Scabies (burrows, finger webs, household contacts itching) (see scabies)
  • Lichen planus, dermatitis herpetiformis, bullous pemphigoid
🩹Drugs / xerosis / psychogenic
  • Drugs (opioids, ACE inhibitors), dry skin (senile xerosis, the commonest cause in the elderly)
  • HIV / cholinergic; psychogenic / delusional parasitosis
  • Diagnosis of exclusion once systemic causes are screened
Rash or no rash? Itch with a primary rash is skin disease. Itch without a rash (only excoriations) means screen the systems — and hunt the red-flag trio of lymphadenopathy, jaundice and weight loss.

Timing and triggers tell. Aquagenic itch (after a hot bath) = polycythaemia; itch of the palms and soles in pregnancy = obstetric cholestasis; itch with night sweats and nodes = lymphoma. Excoriations without a primary rash send you looking at the bloods.

At the bedside — rash or excoriations, nodes and liver, the triggers and timing
History & red flags
Rash or not, distribution, timing (after bathing, at night), weight loss, night sweats, fever (lymphoma), jaundice / pale stools, pregnancy, drugs (opioids), atopy, contacts (scabies), renal / thyroid history, HIV risk
Examine
Look for a primary rash vs only excoriations; check for burrows (finger webs, wrists); lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice; signs of CKD, thyroid disease, and the ruddy face of polycythaemia
Investigate
If no rash: FBC (and film), ferritin, U&E / eGFR, LFTs (ALP / GGT), TFTs, glucose, LDH, and an HIV test; bile acids in pregnancy; chest X-ray / imaging ± lymph-node biopsy if lymphoma is suspected; skin scrapings for scabies

DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash:
A purpuric rash is non-blanching — blood has leaked into the skin (confirm with the glass test). The dermatological question that organises the causes is morphology: is it non-palpable, palpable, or retiform / necrotic? Non-palpable (macular) purpura is a platelet or vessel problem — thrombocytopenia, anticoagulants, or fragile vessels (senile, steroid, scurvy) (see thrombocytopenia). Palpable purpura means inflammation of the vessel wall — a small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein, drug, infection, ANCA-associated) (see vasculitis, paediatric vasculitis). Retiform / necrotic (net-like, angulated, black) purpura signals vessel occlusion — DIC, warfarin necrosis, antiphospholipid, calciphylaxis, cholesterol emboli (see DIC). Over all of this sits the reflex rule: fever + purpura + unwell = meningococcal sepsis → antibiotics now (see meningococcal disease). For the full haematological and systemic work-up of purpura, see the petechiae & purpura note.
🚨Read the shape of the purpura. Fever with a spreading non-blanching rash in an unwell patient is meningococcal sepsis → immediate antibiotics, do not wait (see meningococcal disease). Retiform (net-like) or necrotic purpura is occlusive — think DIC / purpura fulminans (see DIC), warfarin skin necrosis (days after starting) (see anticoagulation), antiphospholipid syndrome, calciphylaxis and cholesterol emboli. Palpable purpura with renal, lung or gut involvement is a systemic vasculitis needing a biopsy and ANCA (see vasculitis). And splinter haemorrhages with fever and a new murmur point to infective endocarditis (see infective endocarditis).

🚩Meningococcaemia / sepsis
  • Fever + a non-blanching purpuric rash + systemically unwell
  • → immediate antibiotics + resuscitation, do not wait (see meningococcal disease, petechiae & purpura)
  • Also septic emboli (endocarditis, other bacteraemia)

  • Net-like, angulated, black purpura = vessel occlusion

  • Coagulation screen, fibrinogen, D-dimer; urgent
🟠Palpable purpura = vasculitis
  • Palpable purpura — small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis
  • Henoch-Schönlein (legs / buttocks + abdo pain + arthralgia + nephritis) (see paediatric vasculitis); drug, infection, ANCA, cryoglobulins (see vasculitis)
  • Skin biopsy + ANCA + urinalysis (check the kidneys)
🟠Thrombocytopenic
  • Non-palpable purpura + low platelets
  • ITP, drug-induced, DIC, marrow failure / leukaemia (blasts) (see thrombocytopenia, leukaemia)
  • FBC + blood film first
🟠Coagulopathy / anticoagulants
  • Warfarin / DOAC / heparin over-anticoagulation, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency (see anticoagulation)
  • Bleeding elsewhere; deranged PT / APTT
  • Review the drug chart and clotting
🩹Non-palpable, non-thrombocytopenic
  • Senile / actinic / steroid purpura (backs of hands / forearms), normal platelets
  • Scurvy (perifollicular, corkscrew hairs), trauma, amyloid
  • Reassure once serious causes are excluded
Feel the purpura, then name the shape. Palpable = vasculitis; flat = platelet / vessel; retiform / necrotic = occlusion. And in the febrile, unwell patient none of this delays meningococcal antibiotics.

DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria:
Urticaria is transient, itchy, raised wheals — each individual lesion lasts <24 hours, blanches, and migrates. It may come with angioedema (deeper, non-itchy swelling of the lips, tongue, eyelids or genitals). Two questions organise it. First, is this anaphylaxis? — wheals with airway, breathing or circulatory compromise mean IM adrenaline now (see anaphylaxis). Second, acute (<6 weeks) or chronic (>6 weeks)? Acute is usually allergic (food, drug, sting — IgE) or post-viral (see urticaria / angioedema). Chronic is spontaneous (autoimmune / idiopathic) or inducible (physical: dermographism, cold, cholinergic, pressure, solar). Two traps: angioedema without weals (ACE-inhibitor or hereditary C1-esterase deficiency — antihistamine-resistant, laryngeal risk) (see drug reactions); and weals that last >24 hours, hurt and bruise — that is urticarial vasculitis (see vasculitis).
🚨Urticaria plus airway or breathing compromise is anaphylaxis. Wheals with lip / tongue swelling, wheeze, stridor or hypotension after a food, drug or sting → IM adrenaline, ABC and remove the trigger (see anaphylaxis). Angioedema without weals is a distinct danger: an ACE inhibitor or hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase-inhibitor deficiency) can cause laryngeal oedema that does not respond to antihistamines / adrenaline in the usual way (see drug reactions). And individual weals lasting >24 hours that are painful / burning and leave bruising or pigmentation are urticarial vasculitis — biopsy and look for connective tissue disease (see vasculitis, connective tissue disease).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Anaphylaxis
  • Wheals + lip / tongue swelling, wheeze, stridor, hypotension
  • Rapid onset after food / drug / sting → IM adrenaline, ABC, remove trigger (see anaphylaxis)
  • Mast-cell tryptase; adrenaline auto-injector + allergy referral
🚩Angioedema without weals
  • Recurrent swelling of lips / tongue / larynx, no itch, no weals
  • ACE inhibitor (stop it) or hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase-inhibitor deficiency, family history, abdominal attacks) (see drug reactions)
  • Antihistamine-resistant — check C1 inhibitor + C4; airway priority
🟠Urticarial vasculitis
  • Individual weals lasting >24 hours, painful / burning, leaving bruising / pigmentation
  • → skin biopsy (leukocytoclastic); associated with SLE / connective tissue disease, hepatitis (see vasculitis, connective tissue disease)
  • Check complement (low), ANA
🟠Acute allergic / viral urticaria
  • <6 weeks; IgE-mediated to food, drug (penicillin, NSAID), sting, latex
  • Or post-viral (commonest in children) (see urticaria / angioedema)
  • Identify and avoid the trigger; antihistamines
🩹Chronic spontaneous urticaria
  • Daily / almost-daily weals for >6 weeks, no external trigger
  • Autoimmune / idiopathic; associated thyroid autoimmunity
  • Non-sedating antihistamines (up-dosed), then omalizumab (see urticaria / angioedema)
🩹Chronic inducible (physical) urticaria
  • Dermographism (weals where the skin is scratched), cold, cholinergic (heat / exercise / sweat)
  • Delayed pressure, solar, aquagenic
  • Confirmed by provocation tests; avoid the trigger + antihistamines
Anaphylaxis first, then the clock. Wheals with airway / breathing compromise = adrenaline. Otherwise ask acute or chronic and hunt the two traps: angioedema without weals and weals lasting >24 hours (vasculitis).

Time each weal. A single lesion lasting <24 hours and blanching is ordinary urticaria; one that lasts >24 hours, hurts and bruises is urticarial vasculitis. And swelling without weals shifts you to angioedema (ACEi / hereditary).

Wheals (raised, blanching, migrating) ± angioedema; dermographism (stroke the skin); check for airway compromise; note lesions that are fixed / bruising (vasculitis) and any systemic signs

DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma:
Erythroderma is redness and scaling affecting >90% of the skin surface — a dermatological emergency in its own right, whatever the cause. The failing skin can no longer regulate temperature or hold fluid: expect hypothermia (or hyperthermia), dehydration, high-output cardiac failure, hypoalbuminaemia and secondary sepsis — so the first job is resuscitate and admit (see dermatological emergencies). Then find the cause. The classic five are eczema, psoriasis, drugs, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Sézary syndrome) and idiopathic (see eczema, psoriasis, lymphoma). Clues to the cause: a pre-existing dermatosis, a recent drug (with fever and eosinophilia = DRESS), lymphadenopathy with circulating Sézary cells, or islands of sparing (pityriasis rubra pilaris). The itch can be intense (see pruritus).
🚨Erythroderma kills through its complications. Widespread vasodilation and barrier loss cause fluid and electrolyte loss, temperature dysregulation (hypothermia), high-output cardiac failure, protein loss (hypoalbuminaemia, oedema) and secondary infection / sepsis — monitor obs, fluids, temperature and skin swabs, and admit (see dermatological emergencies). Look hard for two causes you must not miss: cutaneous T-cell lymphoma / Sézary syndrome (erythroderma + lymphadenopathy + circulating Sézary cells) (see lymphoma) and a drug reaction / DRESS (recent drug, fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia, deranged LFTs) — stop the culprit drug (see drug reactions).

🚩Systemic decompensation
  • Hypothermia / hyperthermia, dehydration, high-output cardiac failure
  • Hypoalbuminaemia, electrolyte loss, secondary infection / sepsis (see dermatological emergencies)

🚩Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Sézary)
  • Erythroderma + lymphadenopathy + intense itch
  • Circulating Sézary cells on the film / flow cytometry (see lymphoma)
  • Skin biopsy + peripheral blood + node assessment
🟠Drug reaction / DRESS
  • Recent drug (1–8 weeks) — anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides
  • Fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia, deranged LFTs = DRESS → stop the drug (see drug reactions)
  • Also simple drug-induced exfoliative erythroderma
🟠Erythrodermic psoriasis
  • Known psoriasis tipping into erythroderma (see psoriasis)
  • Triggers: abrupt withdrawal of steroids, infection, drugs, phototherapy burn
  • May be pustular; look for nail / joint disease
🟠Atopic eczema
  • Long-standing atopic dermatitis flaring to erythroderma (see eczema)
  • Intense itch, lichenification, flexural history
  • Beware superadded infection (bacterial / eczema herpeticum)
🩹Other / idiopathic
  • Pityriasis rubra pilaris (islands of sparing, orange palms / soles, follicular papules)
  • Pemphigus / bullous disease, contact dermatitis (see blistering rash)
  • Idiopathic (“red man syndrome”) — a diagnosis of exclusion
Treat the emergency, then name the cause. Erythroderma is a medical emergency — fluid, temperature and infection come first. Then the cause is usually a pre-existing dermatosis, a drug, or a lymphoma.

History carries the diagnosis. A pre-existing dermatosis or a new drug explains most erythroderma; lymphadenopathy and a suggestive blood film point to Sézary syndrome. A skin biopsy often helps but may be non-specific early.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — the obs and hydration first, then the skin and nodes and drug chart

Pre-existing skin disease (psoriasis, eczema), new drugs (1–8 weeks), speed of onset; fever, rigors, malaise; itch; weight loss, lumps (lymphoma); ability to keep warm and drink
Examine
Extent (>90%), scaling, islands of sparing (PRP), nail / scalp / joint signs (psoriasis); lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly; temperature, pulse, BP, hydration, oedema and signs of skin infection

Admit and resuscitate — warm, rehydrate, correct electrolytes / albumin, treat infection, bland emollients and wet wraps; stop any culprit drug; then treat the cause — topical / systemic therapy for eczema or psoriasis, oncology referral for Sézary syndrome

DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash:
A blistering rash is a fluid-filled eruption — vesicles (<5 mm) or bullae (>5 mm). As always, screen for the emergency first: a painful rash with mucosal erosions and skin detachment is Stevens-Johnson / toxic epidermal necrolysis (see dermatological emergencies); monomorphic punched-out erosions on eczema with systemic upset is eczema herpeticum (see skin infections). Then sort by mechanism. Infective: herpes simplex / zoster (dermatomal), chickenpox, bullous impetigo, staph scalded skin (see viral infections). Immunobullous: bullous pemphigoid (tense, itchy, elderly) and pemphigus vulgaris (flaccid, mucosal, Nikolsky+) (see immunobullous disorders), and dermatitis herpetiformis (itchy, extensor, coeliac) (see coeliac disease). Reaction / physical / metabolic: fixed drug eruption, erythema multiforme, burns / friction, contact dermatitis, porphyria and diabetic bullae. Tense vs flaccid and Nikolsky are the key bedside splits.
🚨Some blisters are emergencies. Skin pain, mucosal involvement (mouth, eyes, genitals), sheets of detachment and a positive Nikolsky sign after a drug = SJS / TEN — stop the drug, treat like a burn (see dermatological emergencies). Monomorphic punched-out vesicles / erosions on eczema with fever = eczema herpeticum (disseminated HSV) → aciclovir; and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and bullous / necrotising infection spread fast (see skin infections, cellulitis). Pemphigus vulgaris (flaccid bullae + mucosal erosions) can be life-threatening from fluid loss and sepsis (see immunobullous disorders).

1Confirm & classify
🚩SJS / TEN
  • Skin pain + mucosal erosions (mouth, eyes, genitals) + sheets of detachment, Nikolsky+
  • A drug trigger 1–3 weeks before → stop it, treat like a burn (see dermatological emergencies)
  • TEN = >30% body surface; ITU / burns care
🚩Eczema herpeticum / disseminated HSV
  • Monomorphic punched-out vesicles / erosions on eczematous skin + fever
  • Disseminated herpes simplex → aciclovir, ophthalmology if periocular (see skin infections, viral infections)
  • Can be fatal in the immunosuppressed
🚩Necrotising / staph scalded skin
  • Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (superficial peeling, children) (see skin infections)
  • Bullous cellulitis / necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, sepsis) (see cellulitis)
  • Rapid spread → antibiotics ± surgery
🟠Pemphigus vulgaris
  • Flaccid bullae that rupture to painful erosions + mucosal involvement, Nikolsky+
  • Intra-epidermal (desmoglein) — biopsy + direct immunofluorescence (intercellular IgG) (see immunobullous disorders)
  • Life-threatening; immunosuppression
🟠Bullous pemphigoid
  • Tense, itchy bullae on an erythematous base in an elderly patient, mucosa usually spared
  • Sub-epidermal — biopsy + DIF (linear IgG / C3 at the basement membrane) (see immunobullous disorders)
  • Topical / systemic steroids
🩹Infective / reaction / other
  • Herpes zoster (dermatomal), chickenpox, bullous impetigo (honey crust) (see viral infections)
  • Dermatitis herpetiformis (itchy, extensor, coeliac) (see coeliac disease); fixed drug eruption, erythema multiforme
  • Burns / friction / oedema blisters, porphyria, diabetic bullae
Tense or flaccid, and Nikolsky? Tense bullae (pemphigoid) sit deeper; flaccid bullae with a positive Nikolsky (pemphigus, SJS / TEN, SSSS) are superficial and dangerous. Always check the mucosae and for a drug.

Distribution and company. Dermatomal = zoster; mucosal + Nikolsky = pemphigus / SJS; tense + itchy + elderly = pemphigoid; extensor + itchy + coeliac = dermatitis herpetiformis. A biopsy with immunofluorescence settles the immunobullous group.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — tense or flaccid, mucosae, Nikolsky, the drug chart

New drugs (1–3 weeks), speed of onset, pain vs itch, mucosal / eye / genital symptoms; atopy (eczema herpeticum), immunosuppression; coeliac / GI symptoms; contact, burns, sun exposure; age
Examine
Vesicle vs bulla, tense vs flaccid, distribution (dermatomal? extensor? photodistributed?); check mucosae, eyes, genitals; Nikolsky sign; estimate body-surface-area involved; are they febrile / unwell?
Investigate
Skin biopsy (histology + direct immunofluorescence) for the immunobullous group; viral swab / PCR (HSV / VZV); bacterial swab; serum antibodies (anti-desmoglein, anti-BP180); tTG for dermatitis herpetiformis; FBC / U&E / cultures if unwell

Treat the emergency — stop the drug and refer SJS / TEN (burns care), aciclovir for eczema herpeticum, antibiotics for infective causes; immunosuppression (steroids ± steroid-sparing) for pemphigus / pemphigoid; gluten-free diet + dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis; wound care and analgesia throughout
